messages.subject: Divergent transitions in "blocker" WinBUGS example
parts:
Hi,

I'm trying to fit the "blocker" Stan model from the WinBUGS example models.  Running this as given (although removing the delta_new line), using the default sampler parameters works (although I get a handful of iterations which hit max_treedepth; increasing this to 15 fixes this).   

The Stan model file uses a t distribution:

  delta  ~ student_t(4, d, sigma_delta); 

Whereas the original WinBUGS model uses a normal. Setting the Stan model to use a normal distribution: 

 delta  ~ normal(d, sigma_delta);   

gives me divergent transitions; typically about 50 after warmup (over the default 2000 total iterations over 4 chains).   I can eliminate these by increasing adept_delta to 0.99 (at the expense of the model running much more slowly)

I've read a few threads on stan-users about divergent transitions, but I'm not sure why I'm seeing them here; it looks like a fairly simple "standard" example.  I'd previously encountered divergent transitions on a more complex network meta-analysis model I was trying to write, except here I wasn't able to eliminate them by increasing adapt_delta (in the end I switched back to JAGS for this, which I'm more familiar with).  

It'd be good to get an understanding of what's going on; can anyone offer any advice?  I realise I can fix the problem for this example by adjusting the sampler settings, but it'd be good to know what it is about the problem that's making it difficult for Stan to solve.  How worried should I be about still (occasionally) hitting max_treedepth? (I've tried setting this even higher, but still get the odd iteration that reaches it).

I've attached the model files I'm running and an R script to run them.

Thanks

David

PS I am getting the occasional warning:
[1] "The following numerical problems occured the indicated number of times on chain 3"
                                                                                   count
Exception thrown at line 23: student_t_log: Scale parameter is 0, but must be > 0!     1
[1] "If this warning occurs sporadically, such as for highly constrained variable types like covariance matrices, then the sampler is fine,"
[2] "but if this warning occurs often then your model may be either severely ill-conditioned or misspecified." 

But as this is only occurring sporadically I'm assuming I shouldn't worry too much about it?

messages.author: 4b681bcd9d4d425d
messages.subject: Re: Divergent transitions in "blocker" WinBUGS example
parts:
Hi David,

I'm definitely not the best person to answer this, though I guess I am the one available first ;)

It looks to me like mu and delta should be constrained both in the variable definition, and the distribution (using, say, lognormal), to be positive. If not, you have a negative standard deviation, which is an obvious no-no, and therefore a model misspecfication. (i.e. "your model may be... or misspecified")

The reason it's happening only occasionally is because those values move away from 0 - since the correct value is obviously higher. Not fixing it shouldn't break anything, but that explains what's going on, if that is clear to you.

Cheers,
David

Yes, they are:

parameters {
....
  real<lower=0> sigmasq_delta; 
....
} 
transformed parameters {
  real<lower=0> sigma_delta; 
  sigma_delta <- sqrt(sigmasq_delta);

Slightly; running the model with a half normal prior on delta, mean 0, standard deviation 10, I get 2.5%, 50%, 97.5% estimates from Stan of:

In WinBUGS with the same prior I get:
0.008 0.125 0.313
Are the divergent iterations during warmup or later?
These are all post warmup (I don't think rstan reports warmup ones).

One way to mitigate the problem is smaller stepsize initially
and higher target acceptance rate.  In RStan, I think it's

  control = list(stepsize=0.01, adapt_delta=0.95)

or something like that.  Or even 0.001 and 0.99 if you still
have problems.  That lowers step size and makes the first-order
approximation to the posterior through the gradient more accurate.

This does help a bit; with stepsize=0.001, adapt_delta=0.99 I get fewer divergent transitions (25 vs 107), and get results closer to WinBUGS's:

0.017 0.131 0.314

There are boundary-avoiding priors that will keep estimates
away from 0, even in maximum likelihood settings.  In realistic
settings, we try to use prior knowledge about the parameter.

Based on prior knowledge it's quite likely its value is 0*, in which case we'd do a fixed-effect meta-analysis, and avoid the issue.  But it also looks like there's quite a lot of support for it being >0. So I'm not sure what the right thing to do would be, given Stan is going to struggle unless we pull it away from 0 via the prior. Using WinBUGS or JAGS seems a bit of a cop-out, but I think it's the route I'll have to go down for now.

Thanks again for your help with this. It's been really useful in working out what's going on.

David

* Turner et al. (2012)  reported 57% of a large sample of meta-analyses had a between study variance of 0 using the method of moments to estimate it.

I did some digging. N=22 here, so I switched to the
non-centered parameterization. That's the critical step in
fitting this (and low N hierarchical models in general) in Stan.
It should also help with Gibbs samplers

I also tightened up the priors in accordance with our current
recommendations (see P.S. below):

data {
int<lower=0> N;
int<lower=0> nt[N];
int<lower=0> rt[N];
int<lower=0> nc[N];
int<lower=0> rc[N];
}
parameters {
real d;
real<lower=0> sigma_delta;
vector[N] mu;
vector[N] delta;
}
model {
rt ~ binomial_logit(nt, mu + d + sigma_delta * delta);
rc ~ binomial_logit(nc, mu);
delta ~ student_t(4, 0, 1);
mu ~ normal(0, 10);
d ~ normal(0, 10);
sigma_delta ~ cauchy(0, 2.5);
}
